claims.text: Partial substitution of Ta and W with V and Cr will reduce the density of the Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr-based alloy.
Controlled annealing can optimize the B2/BCC phase fraction in the proposed Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr-V-Cr system.
A B2/BCC dual-phase microstructure will simultaneously improve room-temperature ductility and yield strength in the proposed alloy.
The baseline is a near-equiatomic Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr alloy in an as-cast or as-sintered state.
The baseline Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr alloy has high density because of Hf, Ta, and W if W is present.
The baseline Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr alloy tends to contain a continuous ordered B2 phase or brittle intermetallics that limit ductility.
Lower-temperature annealing and Cr substitution can promote decomposition of a single ordered B2 phase into ordered B2 and disordered BCC phases.
Annealing must be hot enough to induce B2/BCC decomposition but below the temperature at which brittle Laves or sigma phases form.
Excessive annealing would cause grain growth that is detrimental to the desired properties.
Processing must occur under vacuum or inert gas to prevent oxidation and bulk depletion by oxide-forming impurities such as Mn.
A continuous disordered BCC matrix provides ductility while dispersed ordered B2 provides yield strength.
A fine-grained BCC matrix containing TiO or carbide precipitates can provide grain-boundary and precipitation strengthening without embrittlement.
A continuous ordered B2 matrix is a cause of poor room-temperature ductility in RHEAs.
Disrupting the continuous B2 network should improve ductility.
Fine grains and precipitates can strengthen a BCC RHEA matrix.
The resulting Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr-V-Cr alloy will have more than 1000 MPa room-temperature yield strength and more than 5% total elongation.
The resulting alloy will have a density more than 10% below the baseline.
Formation of brittle intermetallics such as Laves phases would negate the ductility improvement.
Substitution of the heavy elements is assumed not to compromise the high-temperature stability needed for RHEA applications.
Oxygen-derived TiO precipitates may strengthen the alloy but may reduce ductility if they form a continuous network.

contradictions.description: The named baseline composition Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr contains no W, yet W is repeatedly described as a baseline heavy element to be substituted; the named resulting Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr-V-Cr alloy also contains no W. The phrase 'if present' does not specify a consistent W-containing baseline.

The processing conditions broadly frame oxidation and oxide formation as something to prevent, while the proposed mediator includes TiO precipitates as potentially beneficial. The uncertainty field partly qualifies this by distinguishing discrete precipitates from a continuous oxide network, but the desired oxygen boundary condition remains ambiguous.
